claim: Multiple studies have reported a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in males compared to females.
source: Multiple studies have reported a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in males compared to females.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior scholarly work on sex differences in malaria epidemiology.

claim: The study found no evidence of differences in behavioral risk factors by sex.
source: We found no evidence of differences in behavioral risk factors, incidence of malaria, or FOI by sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study comparing behavioral factors between males and females.

claim: The study found no evidence of differences in incidence of malaria by sex.
source: We found no evidence of differences in behavioral risk factors, incidence of malaria, or FOI by sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study comparing malaria incidence between males and females.

claim: The study found no evidence of differences in force of infection (FOI) by sex.
source: We found no evidence of differences in behavioral risk factors, incidence of malaria, or FOI by sex.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study comparing FOI between males and females.

claim: Females cleared asymptomatic infections at a faster rate than males with a hazard ratio of 1.82 (95% CI 1.20 to 2.75) by clone.
source: In contrast, females cleared asymptomatic infections at a faster rate than males (hazard ratio [HR]=1.82, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.75 by clone and HR = 2.07, 95% CI 1.24 to 3.47 by infection event) in multivariate models adjusted for age, timing of infection onset, and parasite density.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of infection clearance data from the cohort study.

claim: Females cleared asymptomatic infections at a faster rate than males with a hazard ratio of 2.07 (95% CI 1.24 to 3.47) by infection event.
source: In contrast, females cleared asymptomatic infections at a faster rate than males (hazard ratio [HR]=1.82, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.75 by clone and HR = 2.07, 95% CI 1.24 to 3.47 by infection event) in multivariate models adjusted for age, timing of infection onset, and parasite density.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of infection clearance data from the cohort study.

claim: Biological sex-based differences are an important factor in the host response to Plasmodium falciparum.
source: These findings implicate biological sex-based differences as an important factor in the host response to this globally important pathogen.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observed differences in infection clearance rates between males and females.

claim: Malaria remains one of the greatest global health challenges.
source: Malaria, a protozoan infection of the red blood cells, remains one of the greatest global health challenges (World malaria report, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the World malaria report, 2019.

claim: In hyperendemic areas, asymptomatic malaria infections are common.
source: Infection with malaria parasites results in a wide range of clinical disease presentations, from severe to uncomplicated; in addition, in hyperendemic areas, asymptomatic infections are common (Bousema et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bousema et al., 2014.

claim: Chronic asymptomatic infection with Plasmodium falciparum can lead to morbidity for those infected.
source: It is well established that chronic asymptomatic infection with Plasmodium falciparum, the most common and fatal malaria parasite, can lead to morbidity for those infected and contribute to ongoing transmission (Bousema et al., 2014; Okell et al., 2012; Tadesse et al., 2018; Slater et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bousema et al., 2014; Okell et al., 2012; Tadesse et al., 2018; Slater et al., 2019).

claim: Chronic asymptomatic infection with Plasmodium falciparum can contribute to ongoing transmission.
source: It is well established that chronic asymptomatic infection with Plasmodium falciparum, the most common and fatal malaria parasite, can lead to morbidity for those infected and contribute to ongoing transmission (Bousema et al., 2014; Okell et al., 2012; Tadesse et al., 2018; Slater et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bousema et al., 2014; Okell et al., 2012; Tadesse et al., 2018; Slater et al., 2019).

claim: Asymptomatic infections represent a major obstacle for malaria elimination efforts.
source: Characterization of these asymptomatic infections is paramount as they represent a major obstacle for malaria elimination efforts.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about malaria elimination challenges.

claim: Age-specific immunity to malaria in hyperendemic areas is well-characterized.
source: While age-specific immunity to malaria in hyperendemic areas is well-characterized, less attention has been paid to the possibility of a sex bias in malarial susceptibility despite evidence for a male bias in malaria infections in non-human animals and a male bias in the prevalence of other human parasitic infections (Zuk and McKean, 1996; Klein, 2004; Roberts et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about malaria immunity.

claim: There is evidence for a male bias in malaria infections in non-human animals.
source: While age-specific immunity to malaria in hyperendemic areas is well-characterized, less attention has been paid to the possibility of a sex bias in malarial susceptibility despite evidence for a male bias in malaria infections in non-human animals and a male bias in the prevalence of other human parasitic infections (Zuk and McKean, 1996; Klein, 2004; Roberts et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zuk and McKean, 1996; Klein, 2004; Roberts et al., 2001.

claim: There is evidence for a male bias in the prevalence of other human parasitic infections.
source: While age-specific immunity to malaria in hyperendemic areas is well-characterized, less attention has been paid to the possibility of a sex bias in malarial susceptibility despite evidence for a male bias in malaria infections in non-human animals and a male bias in the prevalence of other human parasitic infections (Zuk and McKean, 1996; Klein, 2004; Roberts et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zuk and McKean, 1996; Klein, 2004; Roberts et al., 2001.

claim: Pregnant women are at greater risk of malaria infection.
source: The clearest evidence for sexual dimorphism in malaria susceptibility is in pregnant women, who are at greater risk of malaria infection and also experience more severe disease and higher mortality (Desai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Desai et al., 2007.

claim: Pregnant women experience more severe malaria disease and higher mortality.
source: The clearest evidence for sexual dimorphism in malaria susceptibility is in pregnant women, who are at greater risk of malaria infection and also experience more severe disease and higher mortality (Desai et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Desai et al., 2007.

claim: Multiple studies performed in different contexts have demonstrated a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in school-aged children and adults.
source: However, multiple studies performed in different contexts have demonstrated a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in school-aged children and adults (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007); this bias is more well established in hypoendemic areas, but has also been observed in hyperendemic regions (Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007).

claim: The male bias in malaria infection is more well established in hypoendemic areas.
source: However, multiple studies performed in different contexts have demonstrated a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in school-aged children and adults (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007); this bias is more well established in hypoendemic areas, but has also been observed in hyperendemic regions (Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of cited literature.

claim: The male bias in malaria infection has also been observed in hyperendemic regions.
source: However, multiple studies performed in different contexts have demonstrated a male bias in incidence and/or prevalence of malaria infection in school-aged children and adults (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007); this bias is more well established in hypoendemic areas, but has also been observed in hyperendemic regions (Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013.

claim: Differences in malaria incidence or prevalence have often been postulated to stem from an increased risk of males acquiring infection due to socio-behavioral factors.
source: Where there is a male bias in malaria infection, it has often been postulated that these differences in malaria incidence or prevalence stem from an increased risk of males acquiring infection due to socio-behavioral factors (Pathak et al., 2012; Camargo et al., 1996; Moon and Cho, 2001; Finda et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pathak et al., 2012; Camargo et al., 1996; Moon and Cho, 2001; Finda et al., 2019.

claim: Biological sex has been demonstrated to affect responses to other pathogens.
source: However, because biological sex itself has been demonstrated to affect responses to other pathogens, an alternative hypothesis is that the sexes may have different responses to the malaria parasite once infected (Nhamoyebonde and Leslie, 2014; Bernin and Lotter, 2014; Fischer et al., 2015; Fish, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nhamoyebonde and Leslie, 2014; Bernin and Lotter, 2014; Fischer et al., 2015; Fish, 2008.

claim: The study involved 477 children and adults (233 males and 244 females) followed for a total of 669.6 person-years.
source: This analysis involved data from 477 children and adults (233 males and 244 females) that were followed for a total of 669.6 person-years (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study.

claim: 25 participants (10 males and 15 females) were enrolled after initial enrollment.
source: 25 participants, 10 males and 15 females, were enrolled after initial enrollment (Figure 1); median duration of follow-up in those who were dynamically enrolled was 0.84 years (IQR 0.69–1.23) compared to 1.45 years (IQR 1.43–1.47) in those enrolled during initial enrollment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: Median duration of follow-up in those who were dynamically enrolled was 0.84 years (IQR 0.69–1.23).
source: 25 participants, 10 males and 15 females, were enrolled after initial enrollment (Figure 1); median duration of follow-up in those who were dynamically enrolled was 0.84 years (IQR 0.69–1.23) compared to 1.45 years (IQR 1.43–1.47) in those enrolled during initial enrollment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: Median duration of follow-up in those enrolled during initial enrollment was 1.45 years (IQR 1.43–1.47).
source: 25 participants, 10 males and 15 females, were enrolled after initial enrollment (Figure 1); median duration of follow-up in those who were dynamically enrolled was 0.84 years (IQR 0.69–1.23) compared to 1.45 years (IQR 1.43–1.47) in those enrolled during initial enrollment.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: 149 of 477 participants (31.2%) had at least one P. falciparum infection detected.
source: 149 of 477 participants (31.2%) included in the analysis had at least one P. falciparum infection detected (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study and referenced in Figure 1.

claim: 114 participants had 822 successfully genotyped samples and had infections characterized by clone and by infection event.
source: 114 participants had 822 successfully genotyped samples and had infections characterized by clone and by infection event.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study.

claim: 35 samples from 35 unique participants had very low-density infections (<1 parasite/µL) that could not be genotyped.
source: 35 samples (from 35 unique participants) had very low-density infections (<1 parasite/µL) that could not be genotyped; these infections were characterized at the infection event level only.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study.

claim: 92% of genotyped samples achieved a read count of >10,000.
source: We achieved a read count of >10,000 for 92% of genotyped samples, identifying 45 unique AMA-1 clones in our population (frequencies and sequences in Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data from the study.

claim: 45 unique AMA-1 clones were identified in the study population.
source: We achieved a read count of >10,000 for 92% of genotyped samples, identifying 45 unique AMA-1 clones in our population (frequencies and sequences in Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data from the study.

claim: At the clone level, the proportion of baseline infections out of all infections in males was 117/171 (68.4%).
source: At the clone level, the proportion of baseline infections out of all infections in males was 117/171 (68.4%), compared to 68/116 (58.8%) baseline infections in females (p=0.10).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: At the clone level, the proportion of baseline infections out of all infections in females was 68/116 (58.8%).
source: At the clone level, the proportion of baseline infections out of all infections in males was 117/171 (68.4%), compared to 68/116 (58.8%) baseline infections in females (p=0.10).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: At the infection event level, there were 54/104 (51.9%) baseline infections in males.
source: At the infection event level, there were 54/104 (51.9%) baseline infections in males and 45/89 (50.6%) baseline infections in females (p=0.89).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: At the infection event level, there were 45/89 (50.6%) baseline infections in females.
source: At the infection event level, there were 54/104 (51.9%) baseline infections in males and 45/89 (50.6%) baseline infections in females (p=0.89).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no difference in reported rates of LLIN use the previous night by sex.
source: There was no difference in reported rates of LLIN use the previous night by sex (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study presented in Table 1.

claim: Women over the age of 16 traveled overnight outside of the study area more than men (incidence rate ratio for females vs. males = 3.61, 95% CI 1.83 to 7.13).
source: Women over the age of 16 traveled overnight outside of the study area more than men (incidence rate ratio [IRR] for females vs. males = 3.61, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.83 to 7.13), a potential risk factor for malaria exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Antimalarial use outside the study clinic was reported only four times (3 females and one male, all under the age of 5).
source: Antimalarial use outside the study clinic was reported only four times (3 females and one male, all under the age of 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the cohort study.

claim: The incidence of symptomatic malaria was low in all age categories.
source: In this region receiving regular rounds of IRS, the incidence of symptomatic malaria was low in all age categories, and there was no evidence of a difference in incidence of symptomatic malaria by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 1.11, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.52) or when adjusted for age (IRR = 1.26, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.96).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no evidence of a difference in incidence of symptomatic malaria by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 1.11, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.52).
source: In this region receiving regular rounds of IRS, the incidence of symptomatic malaria was low in all age categories, and there was no evidence of a difference in incidence of symptomatic malaria by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 1.11, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.52) or when adjusted for age (IRR = 1.26, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.96).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no evidence of a difference in incidence of symptomatic malaria by sex when adjusted for age (IRR = 1.26, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.96).
source: In this region receiving regular rounds of IRS, the incidence of symptomatic malaria was low in all age categories, and there was no evidence of a difference in incidence of symptomatic malaria by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 1.11, 95% CI 0.49 to 2.52) or when adjusted for age (IRR = 1.26, 95% CI 0.54 to 2.96).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Prevalence ratio of P. falciparum parasitemia by microscopy in females versus males across all age categories was 0.49 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.65).
source: In contrast, prevalence ratio (PR) of P. falciparum parasitemia by microscopy in females versus males across all age categories was 0.49 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.65), with relative differences in prevalence most pronounced in the oldest age group.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Relative differences in prevalence of P. falciparum parasitemia by microscopy were most pronounced in the oldest age group.
source: In contrast, prevalence ratio (PR) of P. falciparum parasitemia by microscopy in females versus males across all age categories was 0.49 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.65), with relative differences in prevalence most pronounced in the oldest age group.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Prevalence ratio of parasitemia assessed by ultrasensitive qPCR was 0.64 in females vs. males (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96).
source: Similar findings were seen when prevalence was assessed by ultrasensitive qPCR, with PR = 0.64 in females vs. males (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96), again with the largest differences seen in the oldest age group.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: The largest differences in qPCR-positive parasitemia prevalence were seen in the oldest age group.
source: Similar findings were seen when prevalence was assessed by ultrasensitive qPCR, with PR = 0.64 in females vs. males (95% CI 0.43 to 0.96), again with the largest differences seen in the oldest age group.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Adjusting for age as a categorical variable, LLIN use, and travel did not qualitatively change prevalence ratios for microscopic parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77).
source: Adjusting for age as a categorical variable, LLIN use, and travel did not qualitatively change prevalence ratios for microscopic parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77) or for qPCR-positive parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.67, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.76).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Adjusting for age as a categorical variable, LLIN use, and travel did not qualitatively change prevalence ratios for qPCR-positive parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.67, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.76).
source: Adjusting for age as a categorical variable, LLIN use, and travel did not qualitatively change prevalence ratios for microscopic parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.57, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.77) or for qPCR-positive parasitemia (PR in females vs. males = 0.67, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.76).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no evidence for a difference in parasite density as determined by qPCR between males and females after adjusting for age as a continuous variable (p=0.47).
source: We also found no evidence for a difference in parasite density as determined by qPCR between males and females after adjusting for age as a continuous variable (p=0.47).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Median complexity of infection (COI) was higher in males than in females overall.
source: Median complexity of infection (COI) was higher in males than in females overall, driven primarily by a higher COI in male school-aged children.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Higher median complexity of infection in males was driven primarily by a higher COI in male school-aged children.
source: Median complexity of infection (COI) was higher in males than in females overall, driven primarily by a higher COI in male school-aged children.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Overall, the force of infection (FOI) was low, with new infections occurring on average less than once every 5 years.
source: Overall, the FOI was low, with new infections occurring on average less than once every 5 years (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study presented in Table 2.

claim: There was no evidence for a significant difference in FOI by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 0.88, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.62 by clone and IRR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.33 by infection event).
source: There was no evidence for a significant difference in FOI by sex overall (IRR for females vs. males = 0.88, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.62 by clone and IRR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.33 by infection event).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no evidence for a significant difference in FOI by sex when adjusted for age category (IRR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.63 by clone and IRR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.31 by infection event).
source: There was also no evidence for a significant difference in FOI by sex when adjusted for age category (IRR = 0.88, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.63 by clone and IRR = 0.83, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.31 by infection event).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was a trend toward higher FOI in males compared to females.
source: For analysis both by clone and by infection event, there was a trend toward higher FOI in males compared to females.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Performing the analysis using one skip for clearance instead of 3 skips increased the FOI in all groups and increased the trend toward higher FOI in males.
source: Performing the same analysis using one skip for clearance instead of 3 skips increased the FOI in all groups and increased the trend toward higher FOI in males, with IRR for females vs. males when adjusted for age category = 0.71, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.24 by clone and IRR = 0.75, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.22 by infection event.
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis of the cohort study data.

claim: Unadjusted hazard ratios for clearing infecting clones showed that asymptomatic infections cleared naturally at nearly twice the rate in females vs. males (hazard ratio 1.92, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.11).
source: Unadjusted hazard ratios for clearing infecting clones showed that asymptomatic infections cleared naturally (i.e., when not treated by antimalarials) at nearly twice the rate in females vs. males (hazard ratio (HR) 1.92, 95% CI 1.19 to 3.11, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study presented in Table 3.

claim: New infections cleared faster than baseline infections.
source: In addition, new infections cleared faster than baseline infections and monoclonal infections cleared faster than polyclonal infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Monoclonal infections cleared faster than polyclonal infections.
source: In addition, new infections cleared faster than baseline infections and monoclonal infections cleared faster than polyclonal infections.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Unadjusted hazard ratios for clearance of infection events showed faster clearance in females vs. males (HR = 2.30, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.42).
source: Unadjusted hazard ratios for clearance of infection events (as opposed to clones) also showed faster clearance in females vs. males (HR = 2.30, 95% CI 1.20 to 4.42).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Higher parasite densities were associated with slower clearance by clone and by infection event.
source: Higher parasite densities were associated with slower clearance by clone and by infection event, but the effect size was larger when data were analyzed by infection event (HR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.54).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: The effect size of parasite density on clearance was larger when data were analyzed by infection event (HR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.54).
source: Higher parasite densities were associated with slower clearance by clone and by infection event, but the effect size was larger when data were analyzed by infection event (HR = 0.44, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.54).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: There was no evidence for interaction between age and sex in either adjusted model.
source: There was no evidence for interaction between age and sex in either adjusted model.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Regardless of whether three skips, two skips, or one skip was used to determine infection clearance, females cleared their infections faster than males both by clone and by infection event.
source: Regardless of whether three skips, two skips, or one skip was used to determine infection clearance, females cleared their infections faster than males both by clone and by infection event (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This claim is supported by sensitivity analysis of the cohort study data.

claim: Durations of infection ranged from 103 days to 447 days by clone.
source: Durations of infection ranged from 103 days to 447 days by clone, and from 87 to 536 days by infection event.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Durations of infection ranged from 87 to 536 days by infection event.
source: Durations of infection ranged from 103 days to 447 days by clone, and from 87 to 536 days by infection event.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Males had a longer duration of infection across all age categories.
source: Males had a longer duration of infection across all age categories.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Children aged 5–15 years had the longest duration of infection, followed by adults.
source: Children aged 5–15 years had the longest duration of infection, followed by adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Males aged 5–15 years had the longest estimated duration of infection by either clone (447 days) or infection event (526 days).
source: Therefore, overall, males aged 5–15 years had the longest estimated duration of infection by either clone (447 days) or infection event (526 days).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: Lower prevalence in females did not appear to be due to lower rates of infection but rather due to faster clearance of asymptomatic infections.
source: We found that lower prevalence in females did not appear to be due to lower rates of infection but rather due to faster clearance of asymptomatic infections.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined findings of similar FOI but faster clearance in females.

claim: This is the first study to report a sex-based difference in the duration of malaria infection.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first study to report a sex-based difference in the duration of malaria infection.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The majority of studies of malaria incidence and/or prevalence that evaluated associations with sex in late childhood, adolescence and adulthood have found a male bias in the observed measure of burden.
source: Though there are some conflicting reports in the literature, the majority of studies of malaria incidence and/or prevalence that evaluated associations with sex in late childhood, adolescence and adulthood have found a male bias in the observed measure of burden (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007; Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Molineaux et al., 1980; Pathak et al., 2012; Landgraf et al., 1994; Camargo et al., 1996; Abdalla et al., 2007; Houngbedji et al., 2015; Mulu et al., 2013).

claim: The male bias in malaria is more often observed in hypoendemic settings.
source: We note that this is more often observed in hypoendemic settings and may be confounded by factors such as treatment-seeking behavior; however, this male bias has been reported in studies of both P. vivax and P. falciparum.
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of cited literature.

claim: The male bias in malaria may be confounded by factors such as treatment-seeking behavior.
source: We note that this is more often observed in hypoendemic settings and may be confounded by factors such as treatment-seeking behavior; however, this male bias has been reported in studies of both P. vivax and P. falciparum.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about potential confounders.

claim: The male bias in malaria has been reported in studies of both P. vivax and P. falciparum.
source: We note that this is more often observed in hypoendemic settings and may be confounded by factors such as treatment-seeking behavior; however, this male bias has been reported in studies of both P. vivax and P. falciparum.
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of cited literature.

claim: Males exhibit higher incidence and/or prevalence of malaria that begins during late childhood, persisting through puberty and the majority of adulthood.
source: Overall, these studies consistently suggest that males exhibit higher incidence and/or prevalence of malaria that begins during late childhood, persisting through puberty and the majority of adulthood (excepting the years when pregnancy puts women at higher risk).
evidence: This claim is based on synthesis of cited literature.

claim: There was no evidence of behavioral trends that would result in more infections in males.
source: We also saw no evidence of behavioral trends that would result in more infections in males; in fact, older women in our study did most of the traveling outside the study area (an area of low transmission compared to surrounding areas).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the cohort study.

claim: The observed male bias in parasite prevalence is best explained by slower clearance of infection in males.
source: Therefore, in this particular cohort, it appears that the observed male bias in parasite prevalence is best explained by slower clearance of infection in males.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined findings of similar FOI but faster clearance in females.

claim: RTS,S vaccination is associated with higher all-cause mortality in girls compared to boys.
source: RTS,S vaccination is associated with higher all-cause mortality in girls compared to boys, and a trend toward higher risk of fatal malaria has been noted in vaccinated girls compared to boys, suggesting possible sexual dimorphism in immunological responses to malaria (Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2016.

claim: A trend toward higher risk of fatal malaria has been noted in vaccinated girls compared to boys.
source: RTS,S vaccination is associated with higher all-cause mortality in girls compared to boys, and a trend toward higher risk of fatal malaria has been noted in vaccinated girls compared to boys, suggesting possible sexual dimorphism in immunological responses to malaria (Klein et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Klein et al., 2016.

claim: The Garki project found a male bias in the prevalence of P. falciparum infection after the age of 5 years that increased after control measures including IRS and mass drug administration.
source: The comprehensive Garki project found a male bias in the prevalence of P. falciparum infection after the age of 5 years that was noted to increase after control measures including IRS and mass drug administration.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Garki project findings.

claim: The Garki project found that females had higher levels of certain antibodies against P. falciparum compared to males.
source: They also found that females had higher levels of certain antibodies against P. falciparum compared to males, but saw no difference in these levels after control measures (Molineaux et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Molineaux et al., 1980.

claim: The Garki project saw no difference in antibody levels between males and females after control measures.
source: They also found that females had higher levels of certain antibodies against P. falciparum compared to males, but saw no difference in these levels after control measures (Molineaux et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Molineaux et al., 1980.

claim: Studies in mice show that testosterone appears to downregulate the immune response to malaria.

claim: Imperfect detection of P. falciparum clones is a limitation of all PCR-based genotyping methods.
source: Imperfect detection of P. falciparum clones is known to be a limitation of all PCR-based genotyping methods; both biological factors, such as deep organ sequestration of clones in the lifecycle of the parasite, and methodological factors, such as difficulty amplifying minority clones (especially at lower parasite densities), results in imperfect detectability of all clones present in a single blood sample drawn on a single day (Felger et al., 2012; Koepfli and Mueller, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2018; Koepfli et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Felger et al., 2012; Koepfli and Mueller, 2017; Nguyen et al., 2018; Koepfli et al., 2011; Ross et al., 2012).

source: Though amplicon deep-sequencing is less likely than other methods to miss minority clones (Lerch et al., 2017), detectability was a particular concern in our study, in which the majority of infections were submicroscopic and parasite densities declined over time [Supplementary file 1c].
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lerch et al., 2017.
